This approach will more closely connect to the universality of human rights, the everyday experiences of affected populations, the pathways through which harm is produced, and the obligation of prevention, access to justice, and effective remedy, as well as accountability. Because rights are enjoyed through the ordinary conditions of daily life, my thematic work will be organized around the systems that secure those conditions, including health and humanitarian action, education, access to information and scientific cooperation, digital infrastructure and technological access, finance, development, debt and sovereign assets, climate resilience, natural resources and disaster response, forced migration, the institution of justice and multilateral cooperation, and recovery after measures are lifted. The geographical scope will reflect the full range of contexts in which these measures have human rights consequences, also comprising less visible contexts, including regional sanctions, regimes, measures whose adverse effects are borne by third states or non-target populations, and patterns of economic coercion that receive limited scrutiny. I will further examine contemporary forms of unilateral measures, that rely on private actors, produce extraterritorial effects, and generate significant spillover. Mr. Vice President, pathways to remedy and restitution must be ensured for affected persons and populations. I will treat remedy as the test of every other commitment. Thank you, Mr. Vice President. Ghana thanks the Special Rapporteur for her timely and substantive report. We align with the statement delivered by the African Group. Thank you.

I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Eritrea.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. Eritrea welcomes the new special rapporteur and wishes her every success in the discharge of her mandate. Thank you.

Thank you.

Thank you.

This was the last speaker we could accommodate for this dialogue. I now give the floor to Ms. Jalad for her concluding remarks. You have six minutes and 45 seconds.

Thank you very much, Mr. Vice President. I would like to thank all states as well as civil society for engaging in this interactive dialogue. Your input is truly invaluable, especially at the start of my tenure. As I mentioned in my statement, this mandate is on the adverse impact of unilateral coercive measures on human rights, what I have called the human cost. I have taken note of the different statements today that have reflected this human cost. In the context from Zimbabwe to Eritrea, Cuba, Iran, Palestine and beyond, people and populations who are far removed from political decision making have borne the heaviest impact of unilateral sanctions. Among those worst affected are the people and populations in vulnerable situations, including, as many of you have mentioned, women, children, older persons, persons with disabilities, with chronic diseases, migrants, refugees, unhoused people, among others. UCMs can never be used as a weapon, and there should not be room to tolerate usage of measures as a tool to suffocate and eradicate a full nation. There should not be room here in this Assembly to accept the usage of UCMs to hold full populations hostages to measures that eradicate and impose forms of slow death of people. As highlighted in my opening statement, this is a moment of truly pronounced strain on the multilateral order. Yet I see a room full of states and stakeholders who are willing constructively to engage with this important mandate, especially during these critical times when the mandate is most relevant and that the engagement is required the most. On the question that was asked on strengthening engagement with states who impose unilateral measures and taking steps to combat the human rights consequences of UCM. I have noted and heard replies. And I take note of these questions. I and on particular the issues that can serve as inroads to better protect the human rights of impacted populations. For example, on the persistent issues of overcompliance, on the issues of de-risking, third states, I intend to use the means and mechanisms at my disposal as well as open door policy to take the opportunities that arise. To the question that was asked on engagement of affected populations, allow me to clarify to the people and populations affected by unilateral sanctions that your voice, your experience, your ideas for change and for effective remedy are those that form the basis of this mandate's analysis. Creating platforms that enable your voices as rights holder to be heard that enable the mandate to document the diverse ways in which your communities experience the consequences of unilateral sanctions, whether human rights, humanitarian, and developmental impact is a priority for my tenure. To the question on the cumulative impact of UCM on the right to development, particularly in developing countries, this is subject that I have identified in my report, noting that unilateral measures depress development and growth. They increase indebtedness and undermine conditions of life for entire populations. We are marking the 40th anniversary of the Right to Development Declaration this year, and in parallel, the mandate is documenting the developmental gains that are reversed by way of unilateral coercive measures. I intend to examine these human rights questions, including thorough analysis that takes into consideration the collective rights to self-determination. I apologize if I was not able to respond to all questions and comments made today. Be assured that I am here for an extended period that will get to address so many other questions and address so many other priorities. And I'm taking into consideration all questions and pointers raised in this forum today. And I look forward to engaging with you. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues, I reiterate, we cannot normalize sanctions and we cannot tolerate the usage of sanctions as a mode of collective punishment. And this should not be tolerated under no condition. No child, no woman should suffer the brunt of the unilateral coercive measures. I wish to thank you sincerely for your productive and encouraging engagement today. I thank you, Mr. Vice President. Thank you.

Thank you.
